opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so there's this line of argument going around that RL isn't really teaching the model anything new. You look at pass@k curves, and if you sample the base model a thousand times it eventually gets the answer, sometimes even more often than the RL'd model at very high k. So people say RL is just reshaping the distribution and isn't adding capability.

I think that undersells it. First, practically, nobody wants to sample a thousand times and then need a perfect verifier to pick the right answer. In most real tasks you don't have that verifier. Being able to get it right on the first or second try *is* the capability. A model that can eventually stumble onto the answer and a model that reliably gets it are very different things to have in the world.

Second, and I think this matters more, these tasks compound. If you're doing something long-horizon, like an agent working through a codebase for hours, you have to make the right call at step one, then step two, then step fifty. Even if the base model has the right action somewhere in its distribution at each step, the probability of chaining all of those together gets vanishingly small. So narrowing the distribution so each step is reliable is what makes long tasks possible at all. The difference between 90% and 99% per-step reliability is enormous over a hundred steps.

Third, once you've narrowed the distribution and the model can reliably do something, that becomes a foundation for the next thing. You can do RL on harder problems that build on the skills it now executes consistently. The base model having something latent is different from the model being able to use it as a building block. A lot of what we're seeing is that the knowledge is in the pretrained model, and RL is the process of making it usable and composable.

And when you look at the models' internals, RL doesn't seem to be inventing whole new circuits from scratch. It's more like it's sharpening and selecting among things that were already there. But that selection is incredibly valuable. Pretraining gives you this enormous soup of possible behaviors and personas, and RL is what turns that into a coherent agent that actually pursues the goal.

r001.rationale: The response says RL narrows the distribution so the model reliably chooses correct actions on real tasks, including long-horizon work where reliable decisions compound.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the pass-at-k framing kind of undersells what's actually happening. People will say, look, if you sample the base model a thousand times, the right answer is in there somewhere, so RL isn't teaching the model anything new, it's just reweighting. And in a narrow sense that's true. But that framing treats the model like a lottery, and nobody wants a lottery. The thing you actually care about is: when I ask once, do I get the right thing?

And the reason narrowing matters is that in the real world, the model doesn't get a thousand attempts with a verifier sitting there telling it which one was correct. Once you're doing something agentic, you're taking fifty, a hundred actions in sequence, and every one of those is a sample. If each step is right ninety percent of the time, you're basically guaranteed to fail over a long horizon. If each step is right ninety-nine point nine percent of the time, suddenly you can do real work. So the capability was latent in the base model, sure, but reliability is the capability for long-horizon tasks. Taking something from one-in-a-thousand to the mode of the distribution isn't a cosmetic change, it's what makes the thing usable at all.

There's also a second piece, which is that the base model has to represent all of that mass somewhere. Pretraining is incentivized to model the whole internet, so a huge fraction of what it knows how to do is imitate confused people, or imitate someone making a plausible-sounding mistake. When you narrow the distribution, you're not just suppressing junk outputs, you're letting the model stop spending compute hedging across personas and modes. And when we look at this from an interpretability angle, you can sometimes actually see that: features that were tracking "what kind of writer is this" become less load-bearing, and the circuits for actually solving the problem get more consistently engaged. So the knowledge might have been there, but the model wasn't committed to using it. RL is partly about commitment.

And then the last thing I'd say is that "the base model could do it given enough attempts" is a statement about the easy cases. For the hard problems, the ones where you need a long chain of correct reasoning, the base model's probability of getting it right is so low that pass-at-k is effectively zero. Narrowing on the easier problems is what builds the behaviors that let you even reach the hard ones. So it compounds. It's not reweighting a fixed set of outputs, it's shifting which outputs are reachable at all.

r001.rationale: The response says narrowing the distribution makes the correct output more likely on a single attempt, improving reliability across long sequences of real-world actions.

astra-6.text:
Because being able to produce the right answer somewhere in the distribution is different from reliably producing it when you need it. If you have to sample a million times to get one correct answer, you still need the compute to generate those attempts and some way to recognize which one is correct. For many tasks, that recognition is itself hard.

Reinforcement learning can move probability mass toward the successful answers. So even if it doesn’t expand what the model could possibly say, it changes what you can practically get out of it with a fixed budget.

And that becomes especially important for tasks that require many steps. If the model has a decent chance of making a mistake at each step, those mistakes compound. Making the useful behavior more reliable can be the difference between occasionally getting a promising fragment and actually completing the task.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning moves probability mass toward successful answers, making useful behavior more reliable and practically obtainable on tasks within a fixed budget.

sol-6.1.text:
Because being able to produce the right answer somewhere in the distribution is very different from reliably producing it. If you need a million samples to get one correct answer, you still have to pay for those samples, and then you have to identify which one is correct. For lots of interesting problems, that second part is itself hard.

So reinforcement learning can take behavior that’s possible but very unlikely under the base model and make it something the model does consistently. Even if you describe that as just narrowing the distribution, that’s a huge practical change. You’re converting this latent capability into something you can actually use.

And that matters even more for long sequences of actions. If you have to make a hundred good decisions in a row, having the right action somewhere in the distribution at every step doesn’t get you very far. You need to put enough probability on those actions that an entire successful trajectory becomes likely.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning makes previously unlikely behavior consistent by putting more probability on useful actions, making the model more reliable and practically usable on tasks.
